concepts.label: Properties of Carbon Compounds and Why Carbon Does Not Form Ions
concepts.cardText: Most carbon compounds are poor conductors of electricity, and from the data on melting and boiling points we find that they have low melting and boiling points as compared to ionic compounds. We can conclude that the forces of attraction between the molecules are not very strong. Since these compounds are largely non-conductors of electricity, the bonding in these compounds does not give rise to any ions. Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell and needs to gain or lose four electrons to attain noble gas configuration. It could gain four electrons forming C4- anion, but it would be difficult for the nucleus with six protons to hold on to ten electrons. It could lose four electrons forming C4+ cation, but that would require a large amount of energy. Carbon overcomes this problem by sharing its valence electrons with other atoms of carbon or with atoms of other elements.

concepts.label: The Covalent Bond: Single, Double and Triple Bonds
concepts.cardText: Many elements form molecules by sharing electrons. Hydrogen has one electron in its K shell and needs one more, so two hydrogen atoms share their electrons to form a molecule of hydrogen, H2; the shared pair constitutes a single covalent bond. Each oxygen atom has six electrons in its L shell and needs two more, so two oxygen atoms share two pairs of electrons, giving a double bond. In nitrogen each atom contributes three electrons, giving three shared pairs and a triple bond. Methane, CH4, is formed because carbon is tetravalent with four valence electrons and shares them with four hydrogen atoms. Bonds formed by the sharing of an electron pair between two atoms are covalent bonds. Covalently bonded molecules have strong bonds within the molecule but weak inter-molecular forces, which gives them low melting and boiling points; since no charged particles are formed they are generally poor conductors of electricity.

concepts.label: Diamond, Graphite and Fullerenes
concepts.cardText: The element carbon occurs in different forms in nature with widely varying physical properties. Both diamond and graphite are formed by carbon atoms; the difference lies in the manner in which the carbon atoms are bonded to one another. In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to four other carbon atoms forming a rigid three-dimensional structure. In graphite, each carbon atom is bonded to three other carbon atoms in the same plane giving a hexagonal array, one of the bonds being a double bond, and the hexagonal arrays are placed in layers one above the other. These two different structures give very different physical properties even though their chemical properties are the same: diamond is the hardest substance known while graphite is smooth and slippery, and graphite is also a very good conductor of electricity unlike other non-metals. Fullerenes form another class of allotropes; the first to be identified was C-60, with carbon atoms arranged in the shape of a football.

concepts.label: Catenation
concepts.cardText: The numbers of carbon compounds known to chemists are estimated to be in millions, outnumbering the compounds formed by all the other elements put together. The nature of the covalent bond enables carbon to form a large number of compounds. One factor is that carbon has the unique ability to form bonds with other atoms of carbon, giving rise to large molecules. This property is called catenation. These compounds may have long chains of carbon, branched chains of carbon or even carbon atoms arranged in rings. No other element shows catenation to the extent seen in carbon compounds: silicon forms compounds with hydrogen with chains of up to seven or eight atoms, but these are very reactive. The carbon-carbon bond is very strong and hence stable, which gives the large number of compounds with many carbon atoms linked to each other.

concepts.label: Tetravalency and the Strength of Carbon's Bonds
concepts.cardText: Since carbon has a valency of four, it is capable of bonding with four other atoms of carbon or atoms of some other mono-valent element. Compounds of carbon are formed with oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and many other elements, giving compounds with specific properties which depend on the elements other than carbon present in the molecule. The bonds that carbon forms with most other elements are very strong, making these compounds exceptionally stable. One reason for the formation of strong bonds is carbon's small size, which enables the nucleus to hold on to the shared pairs of electrons strongly; bonds formed by elements having bigger atoms are much weaker. Tetravalency and catenation together give rise to a large number of compounds.

concepts.label: Saturated and Unsaturated Carbon Compounds
concepts.cardText: Compounds of carbon which are linked by only single bonds between the carbon atoms are called saturated compounds. Ethane, C2H6, and propane, C3H8, are examples: all the valencies of the atoms are satisfied by single bonds. Saturated compounds are normally not very reactive. Another compound of carbon and hydrogen has the formula C2H4 and is called ethene, with a double bond between the two carbons, and C2H2, called ethyne, has a triple bond. Compounds of carbon having double or triple bonds between their carbon atoms are called unsaturated compounds, and they are more reactive than the saturated carbon compounds.

concepts.label: Chains, Branches, Rings and Hydrocarbons
concepts.cardText: Chains of carbon atoms can contain many more carbon atoms than methane, ethane and propane, with 1, 2 and 3 carbon atoms: butane has four, pentane five and hexane six. In addition to straight and branched carbon chains, some compounds have carbon atoms arranged in the form of a ring; for example, cyclohexane has the formula C6H12. Straight chain, branched chain and cyclic carbon compounds may all be saturated or unsaturated; benzene, C6H6, is an example of a ring compound. All these carbon compounds which contain only carbon and hydrogen are called hydrocarbons. The saturated hydrocarbons are called alkanes, the unsaturated hydrocarbons with one or more double bonds are called alkenes, and those with one or more triple bonds are called alkynes.

concepts.label: Heteroatoms and Functional Groups
concepts.cardText: Carbon also forms bonds with other elements such as halogens, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur. In a hydrocarbon chain one or more hydrogens can be replaced by these elements, such that the valency of carbon remains satisfied. The element replacing hydrogen is referred to as a heteroatom. These heteroatoms, and the group containing them, confer specific properties to the compound regardless of the length and nature of the carbon chain, and hence are called functional groups. Important functional groups include halo groups (chloro, bromo), alcohol (-OH), aldehyde, ketone and carboxylic acid. The functional group is attached to the carbon chain through its free valency by replacing one hydrogen atom or atoms.

concepts.label: Homologous Series
concepts.cardText: The presence of a functional group such as alcohol decides the properties of the carbon compound, regardless of the length of the carbon chain. For example, the chemical properties of CH3OH, C2H5OH, C3H7OH and C4H9OH are all very similar. Hence such a series of compounds in which the same functional group substitutes for hydrogen in a carbon chain is called a homologous series. Successive members differ by a -CH2- unit: CH4 and C2H6, and C2H6 and C3H8, differ by one -CH2- unit. As the molecular mass increases in any homologous series, a gradation in physical properties is seen, because the melting and boiling points increase with increasing molecular mass, and solubility in a solvent shows a similar gradation. But the chemical properties, which are determined solely by the functional group, remain similar.

concepts.label: Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds
concepts.cardText: The names of compounds in a homologous series are based on the name of the basic carbon chain, modified by a prefix or a suffix indicating the nature of the functional group. To name a compound, identify the number of carbon atoms: a compound having three carbon atoms would have the name propane. If a functional group is present it is shown in the name with a prefix or suffix. If the suffix begins with a vowel a, e, i, o or u, the final e of the chain name is deleted before adding the suffix; for example propane minus e is propan, plus one gives propanone. If the carbon chain is unsaturated, the final ane is replaced by ene or yne: a three-carbon chain with a double bond would be called propene. The suffix for alcohol is ol, aldehyde al, ketone one and carboxylic acid oic acid, with prefix chloro or bromo for halo alkanes.

concepts.label: Combustion of Carbon and Its Compounds
concepts.cardText: Carbon, in all its allotropic forms, burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide along with the release of heat and light. Most carbon compounds also release a large amount of heat and light on burning; these are oxidation reactions. Saturated hydrocarbons will generally give a clean flame, while unsaturated carbon compounds give a yellow flame with lots of black smoke, leaving a sooty deposit. Limiting the supply of air results in incomplete combustion of even saturated hydrocarbons, giving a sooty flame. Gas and kerosene stoves have air inlets so that a sufficiently oxygen-rich mixture burns with a clean blue flame; if the bottoms of cooking vessels get blackened, the air holes are blocked and fuel is wasted. Fuels such as coal and petroleum contain some nitrogen and sulphur, and their combustion forms oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, which are major pollutants. A flame is only produced when gaseous substances burn.

concepts.label: Oxidation of Alcohols and Oxidising Agents
concepts.cardText: Carbon compounds can be easily oxidised on combustion. In addition to this complete oxidation, there are reactions in which alcohols are converted to carboxylic acids, such as ethanol being oxidised to ethanoic acid. In the activity, alkaline potassium permanganate is added drop by drop to warm ethanol and its colour does not persist at first because it is used up in the reaction. Some substances are capable of adding oxygen to others, and these substances are known as oxidising agents. Alkaline potassium permanganate and acidified potassium dichromate oxidise alcohols to acids, that is, they add oxygen to the starting material, so they are known as oxidising agents.

concepts.label: Addition Reaction and Hydrogenation
concepts.cardText: Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of catalysts such as palladium or nickel to give saturated hydrocarbons. Catalysts are substances that cause a reaction to occur or proceed at a different rate without the reaction itself being affected. This reaction is commonly used in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils using a nickel catalyst. Vegetable oils generally have long unsaturated carbon chains while animal fats have saturated carbon chains. Animal fats generally contain saturated fatty acids which are said to be harmful for health, and oils containing unsaturated fatty acids should be chosen for cooking.

concepts.label: Substitution Reaction
concepts.cardText: Saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive and are inert in the presence of most reagents. However, in the presence of sunlight, chlorine is added to hydrocarbons in a very fast reaction. Chlorine can replace the hydrogen atoms one by one. It is called a substitution reaction because one type of atom or a group of atoms takes the place of another. For example, methane with chlorine in sunlight gives CH3Cl and HCl. A number of products are usually formed with the higher homologues of alkanes.

concepts.label: Properties of Ethanol
concepts.cardText: Ethanol is a liquid at room temperature. It is commonly called alcohol and is the active ingredient of all alcoholic drinks. Because it is a good solvent, it is also used in medicines such as tincture iodine, cough syrups and many tonics, and it is soluble in water in all proportions. Consumption of small quantities of dilute ethanol causes drunkenness, and intake of even a small quantity of pure ethanol, called absolute alcohol, can be lethal; long-term consumption of alcohol leads to many health problems. To prevent misuse of ethanol produced for industrial use, it is made unfit for drinking by adding poisonous substances like methanol and a blue dye; this is called denatured alcohol. Alcohol is also used as an additive in petrol since it is a cleaner fuel which gives only carbon dioxide and water on burning in sufficient air.

concepts.label: Properties of Ethanoic Acid
concepts.cardText: Ethanoic acid is commonly called acetic acid and belongs to a group of acids called carboxylic acids. A 5-8% solution of acetic acid in water is called vinegar and is used widely as a preservative in pickles. The melting point of pure ethanoic acid is 290 K, so it often freezes during winter in cold climates, which gave rise to its name glacial acetic acid. Carboxylic acids are characterised by their acidic nature, but unlike mineral acids like HCl, which are completely ionised, carboxylic acids are weak acids. Like mineral acids, ethanoic acid reacts with a base such as sodium hydroxide to give a salt, sodium ethanoate or sodium acetate, and water.

concepts.label: Esterification and Saponification
concepts.cardText: Esters are most commonly formed by the reaction of an acid and an alcohol. Ethanoic acid reacts with absolute ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst to give an ester, in the esterification reaction. Generally, esters are sweet-smelling substances, used in making perfumes and as flavouring agents. On treating with sodium hydroxide, an alkali, the ester is converted back to alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid. This reaction is known as saponification because it is used in the preparation of soap. Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long chain carboxylic acids.

concepts.label: How Soap Cleans: Micelles
concepts.cardText: Most dirt is oily in nature and oil does not dissolve in water. The molecules of soap are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids. The ionic end of soap interacts with water while the carbon chain interacts with oil. Soap molecules thus form structures called micelles, where one end of the molecules is towards the oil droplet while the ionic end faces outside. This forms an emulsion in water, and the soap micelle helps in pulling out the dirt in water so that clothes can be washed clean. Soaps have two ends with differing properties: one is hydrophilic, interacting with water, and the other hydrophobic, interacting with hydrocarbons. In a micelle the hydrophobic tails are in the interior of the cluster and the ionic ends are on the surface; the oily dirt collects in the centre. The micelles stay in solution as a colloid and do not come together to precipitate because of ion-ion repulsion, and they are large enough to scatter light, so a soap solution appears cloudy.

concepts.label: Hard Water, Scum and Detergents
concepts.cardText: While bathing, foam is formed with difficulty and an insoluble substance, scum, remains after washing with hard water. This is caused by the reaction of soap with the calcium and magnesium salts which cause the hardness of water, so a larger amount of soap is needed. This problem is overcome by using another class of compounds called detergents as cleansing agents. Detergents are generally sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions, and both have a long hydrocarbon chain. The charged ends of these compounds do not form insoluble precipitates with the calcium and magnesium ions in hard water, so they remain effective in hard water. Detergents are usually used to make shampoos and products for cleaning clothes.
